assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and opened relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a redefinition of the second. It is a clean, concrete, lasting advance in precision atomic physics, with a clear discovery (magic-wavelength trapping) and clear instrument.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group drove the systematic-uncertainty and coherence record-setting work. Two names give a natural fair configuration, though Ye's own broader work (also credited under molecules) and contributions by other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Bloom/Ludlow/Ye lineage, Kimble and others) are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: many independent groups worldwide operate and compare optical lattice clocks, intercomparisons agree at the 1e-18 level and the international timekeeping community has adopted them as redefinition candidates. Recognition is timely, not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should instead be shared with ion-clock work, noting Wineland and Hall/Hansch already recognised related technology.
Credit between Katori's original proposal and subsequent group contributions is not fully resolved in the supplied text; I rely on my own recollection of the history, not verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (superfluid-Mott insulator transition, quantum gas microscopes, Hubbard-model engineering) created a controllable platform for strongly correlated many-body physics. The originality is the combination of cold-atom control with proposals to realise Hubbard Hamiltonians, and the impact on both AMO and condensed matter has been wide and durable.
assessment.attribution: The decisive pieces are the Jaksch-Zoller theory of Bose-Hubbard physics in lattices, the Greiner-Bloch-Hansch-Esslinger 2002 Mott transition experiment, and the later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes. Five credited names exceed three laureates; I choose a theory-plus-experiment configuration with Zoller, Bloch and Greiner, which leaves out Esslinger and Cirac, a genuine difficulty in allocation.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a method with broad independent adoption, though headline simulation goals such as the 2D Fermi-Hubbard d-wave phase or fully certified quantum advantage remain open. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Esslinger, Cirac and Hansch-lineage contributors is hard to justify cleanly.
The recognition could be seen as overlapping with the 1997 and 2001 prizes on laser cooling and BEC.
Whether quantum simulation is judged mainly a platform rather than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED mapped cavity QED onto superconducting artificial atoms and microwave resonators, enabling strong coupling, dispersive readout and the transmon-based architecture behind present quantum processors. It is a conceptual transfer with enormous technological and scientific reach.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff produced the 2004 proposal and the first strong-coupling experiments; Blais as theory lead and Wallraff and Schoelkopf as experimental leaders is a sensible three-name set, though Girvin and Devoret-lineage contributions (and the transmon of Koch et al.) are outside the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that many groups reproduced and extended the results for two decades. However, the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so the committee must weigh closeness of subject and the risk of looking repetitive.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize topic and with Devoret, Martinis and Clarke.
Girvin and the transmon developers are not in the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computation began with the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal and became the first platform with high-fidelity entangling gates, teleportation, error-correction primitives and digital quantum simulation. The theoretical proposal is original and the experimental realisation has strong lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the 1995 proposal; Blatt's group performed key entangling, teleportation and simulation experiments. Wineland and Monroe are outside the list (Wineland already honoured 2012), so the three names form a coherent but incomplete picture, with Monroe, Wineland-NIST and Innsbruck contributions interleaved.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with independent commercial and academic systems, though the field's endpoint of scalable fault-tolerant computing is not reached. Recognition would be reasonable but partly overlaps with 2012.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize; absence of Monroe and Wineland-group credit complicates allocation.
Zoller also appears in other candidates, raising a question of how to distribute recognition across entries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new class of band-structure topology with protected edge and surface states, experimentally verified in HgTe wells and Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 crystals. The idea has transformed condensed matter physics and links to the 2016 prize on topological phases.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall effect; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang predicted HgTe; Molenkamp's group observed it; Hasan's group identified 3D topological insulators by ARPES. With four credited names and a three-laureate cap, I choose Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, leaving out Mele (and the credited list does not include BHZ or Zhang), which is an unsettled allocation.
assessment.maturity: Mature after nearly two decades of independent confirmation across materials, with well-understood interpretation. Prize timing is plausible, though the 2016 prize partly overlapped.
uncertainties: Mele and BHZ allocation problem; also parallel candidate on QAH effect.
Overlap with the 2016 Nobel on topological phase transitions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene produced flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable two-dimensional platform, creating the field of moire quantum materials. The theory prediction of the magic angle followed by dramatic experimental confirmation gives it clear originality.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group demonstrated correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018. Eva Andrei's group provided parallel scanning probe evidence of flat bands. A configuration of Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is plausible but excludes Andrei and (not in the list) Dean and Efetov/Kim groups.
assessment.maturity: Fast-moving; the experimental core has been replicated widely, but the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled, and the field is only a few years old, so recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Credit for Andrei and other experimental groups.
Risk of premature recognition relative to older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry for precision measurement of gravity, rotation and constants made matter-wave interference a precision tool, with later uses in tests of the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave detector concepts. The concept is original and the impact in metrology is sizeable.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, Pritchard's early atom interferometer and Kasevich-Chu's light-pulse gravimeter are each decisive, and the three names fit well. Chu and others share related work, and Chu already has a 1997 prize, so the supplied credit seems fair though not exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Technically mature, with commercial gravimeters and independent labs; the large-scale fundamental-physics applications are still developing, so scientific payoff beyond metrology is not yet decisive.
uncertainties: Whether the finding is a single discovery or a collection of techniques.
Partial overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution transformed quantum information into a practical cryptographic protocol, with BB84 and E91 supplying conceptual foundations that link Bell nonlocality to security. The ideas are original and lasting, with growing real-world deployment.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard created BB84; Ekert proposed the entanglement-based protocol. Pan's experimental satellite and long-distance work is also credited, but with four names and a three-laureate cap I propose the three theorists, leaving experimental demonstrations unrecognised, a real allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Conceptually mature, though practical security under device imperfections and deployment relevance are still debated; part of the foundations were recognised by the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on Bell tests.
Excluding Pan and experimental credit may be contested.
Practical security of implementations remains debated.
